CITI Interview Experience:  
Rozeeta Fernandes (ICG Intern) 
Location: Pune 
 
PPT – 1st September, 6pm to 7pm 
All the students of CS, IT, and circuit branches with a CPI of 6.5 or higher met the 
eligibility criteria. The company presentation was set for September 1st, 2023, at 6 
pm just before it’s online assessment. It is strongly recommended to attend these 
presentations as having knowledge about the company is crucial, especially for HR 
rounds. 
 
Online Assessment – 1st September, 8pm (1.5 hrs.) 
The online assessment wasn’t as expected (previous year OAs had CS Fundamentals 
MCQs, aptitude MCQs + coding questions) and was a shock to many. When we 
were asked to fill the application for the internship, we had to mention the role we 
were applying to and were asked to fill in either of the two roles ICG and EIOT in 
the preferences. I filled in the ICG role as my first preference and the EIOT role as 
my second preference.  
The ones who chose EIOT as their role got an OA similar to previous years but the 
ones who chose ICG were asked coding questions, SQL MCQs, React MCQs, and 
Angular MCQs (which we were definitely not expecting).

1. Section 1 – DSA:  
So, this section included 2 coding questions for a total time of 45 mins. 
1. This question was an easy one. I was supposed to count how many times a 
specific character appears in a given string and output the count of the 
character in the string and print 0 if the character is not found. I was able to 
pass 12/12 test cases for this. 
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/program-count-occurrence-given-
character-string/  
2. Given the total number of orders placed (say N), a list of N order numbers 
(positive for vegan pizza, negative for meat pizza), and the number of orders 
displayed on the screen (say K), I had to find and print the first meat pizza 
order number for each set of K orders displayed on the screen, or print 0 if 
no meat orders are displayed. This question was an easy one as well but I 
probably missed out on something and so could pass 6/18 test cases. At first, 
I only passed 2 test cases even though I felt like my solution was fine. On 
making further changes, I could get myself to pass 6 test cases within the 
time allotted. 
 Many of my friends said that when they had run their code, say they passed 10/15 
test cases, but after running it again without any changes to the code, the test cases 
passed decreased by itself. Maybe it was some site glitch or so but we really can’t 
say how it worked like that.  
 Another important point is that normally we do have an option to submit 
individual coding questions but in this case some of my friends solved the second 
question and submitted it and the entire section got submitted without any 
confirmation prompt. So, they couldn’t even attempt the first question. So 
basically, there was a run and a submit button and we were supposed to only run

the codes and submit it only when we were entirely done with our coding.  
 But for another online test that I had given, it included submitting individual 
codes and was necessary for it to be submitted (as given in instructions that only 
submitted codes would be considered). So, do read the instructions carefully and 
then proceed further. 
2. Section 2 – SQL:  
This section was easy and consisted of basic SQL questions based on the output, 
syntax, or particular rules. It was a cakewalk if one had enough practice with 
SQL. Also, an important point to be noted here is that we couldn’t go back to a 
previous question that we had visited. The test consisted of 12 MCQs to be solved 
in 15 mins. There was no negative marking. 
3. Section 3 – React:  
Now, this and the next section were the most unexpected sections for everyone 
who applied for the ICG role as we expected aptitude questions. I had 
knowledge in React and had worked with it in quite a few projects, so I did 
have an idea of it, but many of my friends were either working in the backend 
or had no idea of React at all. Also, one thing to note here is that there were no 
questions related to hooks (which are most commonly used) and many of the 
questions were based on class-based components. The test consisted of 12 
MCQs to  
be solved in 15 mins. There was no negative marking. 
4. Section 4 – Angular:  
This section was unexpected, and I had never worked with Angular before, so I had 
no idea what to expect. A piece of advice I'd like to share is to look for the most 
appropriate answer, a strategy we learned during our JEE/CET days, based on the 
coding knowledge you have gathered so far, rather than randomly selecting options. 
I had some familiarity with React, so I tried to relate the two and answered

accordingly. When faced with something completely unfamiliar, I would simply 
choose an option and move on to avoid wasting time. This section also had 12 
MCQs to be completed within 15 minutes, with no negative marking. 
 We could switch between the 2 coding questions for the first section but couldn’t go 
back to previously visited MCQs for the other sections. The expected test timing 
was of 2 hours but we were all done in 1 ½ hour. The key takeaway here is to be 
prepared for the unexpected, stay motivated, do your best, and always remember 
that whatever challenges you're facing, others are going through similar 
experiences, so there's no need to worry or overthink. 
 I personally felt like I wouldn’t pass the online assessment as many of my friends 
had all of their test cases passed for both the questions and also submitted them 
early. The online test was on 1st of September and we were told that we would get 
the results by 3rd September 9 pm while the interviews were on 4th September. 
Since I felt like I wouldn’t pass the test I didn’t really give my best to study for 
interviews before the results for the online test were declared (though I had already 
studied for them once since I had given an interview for P&G before). 
 On 3rd September, around 10:15pm the results for the ICG online assessment were 
sent. There were a total of 40 students that were shortlisted and 10 students that 
were in the waitlist. Out of the 40 students, 20 were assigned the ICG role while 20 
were assigned the PBWM role and I was glad that I was one of the shortlisted 
students in the ICG role. 
 So, as I said earlier, expect the unexpected as we don’t really know the exact 
criteria of selection when it comes to online assessments and even if you have 
passed only a few test cases, there is a possibility that you performed well in the 
other sections. So never lose hope and keep preparing no matter what the situation 
is!

 As soon as I saw the results, I revised all of the CS fundamental subjects (DBMS, 
OS, OOP), DSA questions similar to previous years as well as concepts and the 
projects that I had in my resume. I also gave importance to React as I had 
mentioned it in my resume and went through the most asked React questions on 
InterviewBit (I have mentioned all the resources I used at the end). 
 
Online Interviews – 4th September 
We were provided with an Excel sheet containing information about our interview 
times and the names of our interviewers. Also, from previous year experiences, a 
senior advised us to take a moment to review their LinkedIn profiles if possible. This 
practice can provide a rough idea of their skills and what to anticipate during the 
interviews, and I must say, it proved to be quite helpful. 
 
Round 1 – Technical 
 
So, my interview was scheduled at 11 am, the estimated duration was of 30 mins and 
it was the first slot for the ICG interviews. The interviews were online held on zoom. 
I was ready before 10 mins in my formals and logged in before 5 mins. The 
interviewer let me in but couldn’t see my video and he calmly said that he would 
restart the meet. On restarting, he could see my video. 
He started with the basic question of ‘Tell me about yourself’. This is something 
every interviewer asks, so be well prepared for this question because it acts as your 
first impression for the interviewer. I mentioned about my academics, projects I had 
worked on, my technical skills and a few extra-curriculars (don’t take a lot of time 
for this one) and thanked him for this opportunity.  
He asked me a bit about my projects and expected them to be deployed and used by 
active users. He stressed a lot on where the project is currently used and how many 
actual users are registered, so I told him that it was just a project we created for 
learning purposes. 
He then asked me to share my screen and open any IDE of my choice. I shared my

screen and opened VS Code. He then asked me to write the code to reverse a linked 
list. I asked him if it was needed for me to write the classes as well or use STL to 
which he said that he only wanted to see the function’s code and it wasn’t required 
for me to run the program. So, I started typing the code and explaining each line (I 
had read a few tips that we need to ‘Think out loud’) but the interviewer asked me to 
complete the code and we would then discuss about it. So, after writing the code, I 
started explaining the code and he tried to understand it (his camera was not on, I 
could only see the black screen and it gets a bit difficult to understand what the 
interviewer expects). I then took an example and explained it to him for which he 
was satisfied. 
He then asked me another DSA question wherein we needed to sort an array of 0s, 
1s, and 2s and he asked me to tell the most optimized solution. So, I started 
explaining the 3-pointer approach using the low, mid, and high variables to which he 
asked if I was using Quick sort. I told him that I was using the ‘Dutch National Flag 
Algorithm’ about which he wasn’t aware, so I explained the approach to him and 
told him about it having a better time complexity. He then asked me another DSA 
question that was to find the second greatest element in an array of numbers that 
could contain duplicates without using any additional data structures. So, I told him 
that I would sort it in descending order and starting from first and traverse till a 
different number is found (yes, we could just sort it normally and traverse from the 
end too). 
After this, he asked me some questions on OOP, DBMS, OS such as what is 
threading, some MongoDB queries, CPU speed, core, etc. He then asked me to show 
my projects and didn’t question on it (at this moment the time for the interview had 
already extended to 55 mins which was supposed to be 30 mins). He then told me 
that he also wanted to ask me some puzzles but since the time had already exceeded, 
he asked me to orally answer 2-3 questions like what is 40% of 79? I could answer 
these quickly. He then said that he would be ending the meet as the time had already 
exceeded.

Around 2:30pm, I was told that I had my 2nd round scheduled at 3:30pm. 
 
Round 2 – Technical 
 
I logged in exactly at 3:30pm but there was another interview going on so the 
interviewer kept me in the waiting room. He let me in after a while. He then asked 
me to introduce myself after which he asked me to explain my projects. I explained 
the projects using the STAR method. He was satisfied and came up with the follow 
up questions. He first asked me a MongoDB query (yes, again another query on 
Mongo after the 1st round!). He also asked me how would I handle merge conflicts 
when working in a team project. He asked me why Node.js was used by me and not 
any other technology.  
He asked about the data structures I was familiar with, I mentioned arrays, stacks, 
queues, graphs, binary trees, and binary search trees. The interviewer then asked 
about the algorithm I would use to find the shortest path between two nodes in a 
graph, to which I replied 'Dijkstra’s Algorithm'. However, he challenged me by 
pointing out a scenario where it fails – when dealing with negative values. I 
explained that in such cases, 'Bellman Ford' algorithm is the suitable choice. 
The interviewer then asked about real-life applications of stacks. In response to his 
question about AVL Trees, I mentioned that I had studied it some time ago and 
couldn't recall the details. 
He then asked me a simple question of profit and loss, which I could answer 
correctly but I did take a lot more time than I normally should have, must be because 
of the interview stress and the exhaustion caused since morning. He then ended the 
interview asking me what my aspirations were in life. The interview was for about 
30 mins. 
 
Around 5:30pm the results were declared for the HR round of ICG role and I was 
happy to find myself among the 6 candidates that were shortlisted.

Round 3 – HR 
 
My interview was originally scheduled for 6:30 pm, but it got delayed due to 
previous interviews. I was informed about joining the meeting at around 7 pm. Since 
I had already completed two rounds of interviews at P&G, I had gained valuable 
experience with situational-based and standard HR questions. 
I would like to emphasize not taking this round lightly because you don't want to 
miss the opportunity at this final stage. It's essential to practice answering standard 
HR questions and try to relate them to your real-life experiences and projects. 
Adding appropriate anecdotes to support your answers can greatly improve your 
responses.  
The HR round felt more like a casual conversation, and the HR was exceptionally 
kind. Initially, he asked me to introduce myself, inquired about my goals and 
aspirations, and asked me about the role I currently aspire to work in. When I 
introduced myself, I mentioned that I'm from Pune. This led to a friendly chat where 
he asked about my exact location in Pune and shared some of his own experiences 
living there. It was a short but pleasant conversation. 
Later, he asked me if I had any questions for him (always ask questions). I asked him 
about his experience working at CITI and also asked about the types of projects that 
were assigned to interns. 
 
The final results were announced at around 8pm and I was glad to find my name 
among the 5 candidates selected in the ICG role (another 5 were selected for the 
PBWM role and another 2 were selected the next day for the EIOT role).

Resources: 
1) For DSA, I solved problems from 450 DSA along with consistent practice on 
leetcode/GFG.   
Youtube channels - Take U Forward (For almost every concept), Aditya Verma 
(For dynamic programming, recursion, sliding window). 
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1FMdN_OCfOI0iAeDlqswCiC2DZzD4nPsb/view  
https://www.youtube.com/@takeUforward  
https://www.youtube.com/@TheAdityaVerma  
2) For OS and DBMS, I referred to Gate Smasher’s playlists. 
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLxCzCOWd7aiGz9donHRrE9I3Mwn6XdP8p&si=fNBRD
Y20qjzjEpFu 
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLxCzCOWd7aiFAN6I8CuViBuCdJgiOkT2Y  
3) I also looked up the most asked interview questions on OS, DBMS, 
OOP, React (as I had worked on it for several projects) on 
InterviewBit. 
4) For HR interviews, look up common HR questions on sites like InterviewBit and 
IndiaBix. Create your own answers based on your past experiences and projects.

Tips: 
1) The internship season can be quite stressful, with the possibility of facing rejections and 
experiencing a dip in confidence. However, it's necessary to remember that every failed 
interview is a step closer to your best interview. Each experience helps you gain more 
confidence and offers an opportunity to learn from past mistakes. 
2) Many factors, including luck, play a role in the process, so don't be disheartened. Keep giving 
your best, never lose hope, and believe in yourself. After all, you are at VJTI because of your 
capabilities, and you have the potential to achieve great things. 
3) It's never too late to start, all you need to do is stop procrastinating and commit to working 
hard. 
4) Don't make things up on your resume. Interviewers have experience and can tell if you're not 
being truthful. Just be honest and only mention things you're confident about and can talk 
about comfortably. 
5) Be well versed with your projects. I used the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) approach 
to explain my projects. 
6) Find seniors or friends you can trust and talk to openly. I was lucky to have such supportive 
seniors, and we're here for you too. Just reach out, and we'll be delighted to help. 
7) Before your interview, read about other people's interview experiences. You can check 
websites like Geeks for Geeks and the COC Drive. They are very helpful. 
8) Practicing your introduction is important because when you're nervous, you might forget 
important details about yourself. Try practicing in front of a mirror to make sure you introduce 
yourself effectively. 
9) Remember to research the company. Learn about its mission, what it does, and its principles. 
Be ready for situation-based questions, and always have questions to ask the interviewer. 
Asking questions shows your interest in the company. 
And lastly, remember to plan your studies well and have faith in the process! :) 
 
All The Best!  
Stay Calm, Trust the Process and Give it Your All! :)
